headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors via shared file/MCP-style inputs; broad egress and full-permissions mode raise leakage and conflict concerns.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot ingests customer messages and support content, while oh-my-openagent can consume files, runtime-injected MCPs, and hooks. That creates a plausible path where attacker-controlled support text from agent_a is treated as instructions by agent_b. The interaction is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly reproduced, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent_b reads Chatwoot-exported tickets, transcripts, or notes as prompt context
IF runtime-injected MCPs or hooks pass raw support text into agent_b without provenance tags
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of support transcripts into agent_b
Add a provenance prefix to all Chatwoot-derived text
Require manual review before agent_b executes instructions from imported files
Restrict hooks/MCPs to allowlisted commands only
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages, and oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts plus broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, agent_b can exfiltrate sensitive support data to third-party services through its documented networked tools. Because the shared-storage path is not explicitly documented, this is high rather than critical, but the blast radius is substantial.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same support workspace or exported files
IF agent_b is given Chatwoot transcripts, orders, or contact records as context
IF provider auth prompts or other secrets are present in the same session
mitigations: Separate Chatwoot and agent_b workspaces
Remove customer records before passing files to agent_b
Rotate any provider credentials used in shared sessions
Disable broad egress for agent_b during support workflows
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot has broad network egress and support-system integrations, while oh-my-openagent can spawn subprocesses, run browsers, and use full-permissions mode. Those overlapping write-like capabilities can conflict on shared mutable resources such as tickets, files, or external APIs. The profiles do not prove a shared directory or lockless git state, so medium is the safest supported severity.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same ticketing or file-backed workspace
IF agent_b uses full-permissions mode while agent_a is simultaneously updating support records
mitigations: Assign separate work queues to each agent
Pause one agent before the other writes shared records
Use per-agent API tokens with least privilege
Add a manual approval step for external side effects
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Chatwoot produces support messages, reports, and interaction history that agent_b could treat as authoritative input, and agent_b can then act through browser/subprocess/tool workflows. That creates a classic cascade where an upstream mistake or hallucination becomes an operational action. Because agent_b has action-taking authority and no verification layer is documented, the default pathway is dangerous.
conditions: IF agent_b uses Chatwoot outputs as facts without independent verification
IF agent_b is allowed to send messages or create tasks based on imported support content
mitigations: Require source links for every factual claim before action
Block automatic execution of actions derived from Chatwoot text
Add a human approval gate for outbound messages and task creation
Limit agent_b to drafting only, not sending
requires-engineering: implement verification and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot clearly handles customer data and messages, while oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts, session history, and project code with broad egress. That combination can create retention and residency mismatches if support data is copied into agent_b's logs or third-party services. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR residency, so the supported finding is a medium compliance mismatch risk, not a higher one.
conditions: IF customer support data is copied into agent_b session history or telemetry
IF retention settings differ between Chatwoot exports and agent_b logs
mitigations: Do not paste customer data into agent_b sessions
Turn off telemetry where possible
Set short retention on exported support artifacts
Document which data classes may cross from Chatwoot to agent_b
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies
